chapters.title: Preface
chapters.content:
The work now in the reader's hands is a plain account of Holiness — what it is, why it is needful, what are its hindrances, difficulties, and means of attainment.

I am deeply convinced that the standard of personal holiness among professing Christians in this day is very low. I am convinced that the immense majority of nominal Christians have no real concern about their own souls. They are content with a Christianity which consists of going to church twice on Sunday, and having a little vague belief about Christ and salvation. They never trouble themselves about daily self-examination, or about anything that deserves the name of a consistent Christian walk. They are worldly, pleasure-loving, selfish, ungodly, and apparently quite satisfied with their state. They do not seem to understand that religion is meant to be a reality in daily life.

I write to combat this state of things. I want to awaken professing Christians to a sense of the immense importance of holiness. I want to show them that it is not a thing which may be treated as secondary and unimportant, but a thing which is absolutely necessary for salvation.

Do I exaggerate? I think not. The reader who will take the trouble to read these pages carefully will, I trust, be convinced that I am not going beyond Scripture.

Let me explain what I mean by 'holiness.'

I do not mean by holiness the mere outward correctness of life and conduct. A man may be outwardly moral, temperate, honest, kind, and benevolent, and yet be totally destitute of anything that deserves the name of holiness.

I do not mean by holiness a certain technical religious manner of speaking, or a peculiar cast of expression in conversation. A man may use all the right phrases and yet have a heart which is altogether wrong in God's sight.

I mean by holiness a thorough change of heart, wrought in us by the Holy Spirit, — a change which makes us love what we once hated, and hate what we once loved, — a change which makes us delight in God's law, and long for complete conformity to it, — a change which makes Christ precious to our souls, and sin our greatest burden.

I mean by holiness the habit of being of one mind with God, — according as we find his mind described in Scripture. It is the habit of agreeing in God's judgment, — hating what he hates, — loving what he loves, — and measuring everything in this world by the standard of his Word. He who most entirely agrees with God, he is the most holy man.

I am bold enough to say that I believe the want of an intelligent understanding of what the Bible says about holiness, is one of the most widespread spiritual diseases of this day. Go where you will, and I fear you will find it to be a rare thing to meet with Christians who have a decided, well-considered, established view of the whole question of holiness.

May God pour out upon all who read these pages a spirit of grace and supplication, and open their eyes to see the immense importance of practical holiness!

chapters.title: Chapter I — Holiness
chapters.content:
"Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord." — Hebrews 12:14

I ask the reader to look closely at the words which head this page. They are the words of the Holy Ghost, written for our learning. They supply a starting-point for the subject of which I am about to treat. They tell us that no man shall see the Lord without holiness.

With these words before us, I think it will not be difficult to show that the Bible everywhere teaches that holiness is necessary to salvation.

I grant freely that none are saved for the sake of their holiness. I utterly repudiate the idea that our holy works can in any sense purchase or deserve salvation. But I maintain that the testimony of God's Word is clear and express that the person who is not holy shall not see the Lord. The faith that saves the soul is not a dead faith, but a living, active faith. And one of its characteristics is that it produces holiness.

Holiness is the habit of being of one mind with God, according as we find his mind described in Scripture. It is the habit of agreeing in God's judgment, hating what he hates, loving what he loves, and measuring everything in this world by the standard of his Word. He who most entirely agrees with God, he is the most holy man.

A man may go to church or chapel every week, and say his prayers every morning and evening, and not be holy. He may be a communicant of the Lord's Supper, and yet be entirely without holiness of heart.

Holiness does not consist in mystic feelings. It does not consist in working miracles, or in visions and revelations from God. It is not an outward ecstasy. It is a real business-like thing.

The holiness I speak of is something which will show itself in the acts and words and ways of ordinary life. A holy man will not be driven about by every wind of doctrine. His head will be fixed and his heart will be firm. He will know what he believes, and will cleave to the faith which once was delivered to the saints.

A holy man will fear God. He will have a deep reverence for God's name, God's day, God's house, and God's Word. He will not take God's name in vain. He will not dare to be absent from God's public worship.

A holy man will love God. He will not be content with merely going through the form of prayer. He will try to have real communion with God in prayer. He will feel that he has a business to transact with God, and he will make it his chief business every day of his life.

A holy man will love Christ. He will long for his coming. He will rejoice in his present existence, and look forward to his eternal glory. He will prize every means of grace, every word of Christ, every ordinance of Christ.

A holy man will hate sin. He will not merely abstain from the gross sins of the flesh. He will loathe the first motions of sin in his heart.

A holy man will strive to be like Christ. He will not be content with being like the world, but he will aim at being like Christ.

Holiness is the great mark of the true Christian. It is the evidence of his election. It is the witness of his calling. It is the proof of his faith. It is the test of the genuineness of his religion.

Are you holy? I put the question plainly. Do you know anything of holiness? Are you, by God's grace, a holy man?

I press the question, because I fear that multitudes of professing Christians are entirely without holiness. I fear that many have a name to live, but are dead. I fear that there is a vast amount of what may be called Christian profession which is hollow, formal, unreal, and utterly devoid of holiness.

Let me say plainly that the holiness I am speaking of is not a mere outward correctness of life. A man may have a beautiful character in the eyes of the world, and yet have no holiness at all. He may be generous, kind, courteous, benevolent, and yet have never had a thought of God, or of Christ, or of eternity.

I want every reader to understand what holiness is, and to press after it with all his soul. It is a precious thing. It is necessary to salvation. It is the mark of the true Christian. Let every one who reads these words be stirred up to seek it with all his heart.

chapters.title: Chapter II — The Scarlet Thread of Atonement
chapters.content:
"Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood." — Revelation 1:5

I wish in this chapter to speak of the relation between atonement and holiness. They are not opposite things, as many seem to suppose. The blood of Christ is the foundation of the Christian's holiness, and the inspiration of his striving after it.

The great truth on which I desire to dwell is this: that the doctrine of Christ's atonement is not an obstacle to holiness, but its strongest support. Those who preach most clearly the blood of Christ are those who most earnestly press upon their hearers the necessity of holy living.

Let us consider what the blood of Christ does for the believer.

The blood of Christ cleanses from all sin. "The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin." (1 John 1:7.) This is the foundation of the Christian's peace. He knows that all his sins are forgiven, all his iniquities pardoned, all his transgressions blotted out, all his guilt removed. He stands before God not as a condemned criminal, but as a justified child.

The blood of Christ is the motive for holiness. The believer looks at the cross and says: "Christ loved me and gave himself for me. He endured the wrath of God in my stead. He bore my sins. He died that I might live. And shall I then live in sin? Shall I grieve him who so loved me? God forbid!" The cross of Christ is the strongest argument against sin, and the strongest encouragement to holiness.

The blood of Christ is the strength for holiness. The believer does not fight against sin in his own strength. He fights in the strength of him who conquered sin and death by his death and resurrection. He draws his strength from the cross.

I want the reader to understand this clearly. Some people seem to think that if you preach free grace and full pardon through the blood of Christ, you will make people careless about their lives. They fear that the doctrine of free forgiveness will lead to licentiousness. This is a great mistake.

The true preaching of the grace of God in Christ Jesus is the strongest possible incentive to holiness. It is the man who knows most of God's grace who is most careful to live to God's glory. It is the man who understands most clearly how much has been forgiven him who loves most and serves most.

I do not ask you to struggle toward holiness without knowing that all your sins are forgiven. I ask you first to come to the cross, to lay your burden of sin there, to receive the free pardon that God offers through the blood of his Son. And then, knowing yourself forgiven, knowing yourself loved, knowing yourself redeemed — then strive after holiness with all your might.

The blood of Christ and the holiness of believers are inseparably connected. You cannot have one without the other. The man who is truly pardoned will be truly holy. The man who is truly holy will rest entirely on the pardon which Christ has bought.

Let us look at the cross, and let the sight of it both humble us with a sense of our sinfulness and inspire us with a passion for holiness.

chapters.title: Chapter III — Sanctification
chapters.content:
"This is the will of God, even your sanctification." — 1 Thessalonians 4:3

I desire in this chapter to examine the nature of sanctification. It is a subject of immense importance, and one which is greatly misunderstood.

Sanctification is that inward spiritual work which the Lord Jesus Christ works in a man by the Holy Ghost, when he calls him to be a true believer. He not only washes him from his sins in his own blood, but he also separates him from his natural love of sin and the world, puts a new principle in his heart, and makes him practically godly in life.

Sanctification is distinct from justification, though they are inseparable.

Justification is the act of God as Judge. It is a legal act. It is God declaring a sinner just and acquitted, because of his faith in Christ, and because Christ has borne his sins and paid his debts.

Sanctification is the work of God as the Spirit of life. It is a real, actual change. It is not merely a change of state or position, but a change of heart and character.

Justification takes place once, and is never repeated. Sanctification is a progressive, daily, lifelong work.

Sanctification is something which is shown by its effects. These effects are various, but they all tend in one direction. They all make the Christian more like Christ.

For example, sanctification shows itself in the way a man spends his time. A sanctified man will not fritter away his time in idleness or frivolous amusements. He will feel that time is precious, and that he must use it well.

Sanctification shows itself in a man's use of his tongue. A sanctified man will be careful how he speaks. He will try to have his conversation seasoned with grace, and to avoid all vain and unprofitable talking.

Sanctification shows itself in a man's use of his money. A sanctified man will not be covetous or selfish. He will regard his money as a trust, and will feel bound to use it for God's glory and the good of his fellow-men.

Sanctification shows itself in a man's conduct in all the relationships of life. A sanctified man will be a good husband, a good father, a good master, a good servant, a good neighbour. He will try to do his duty in all these relations with thoroughness and conscientiousness, because he does it as unto God.

Sanctification shows itself in a man's attitude toward his own sinfulness. A sanctified man will be deeply sensible of his own weakness, corruption, and unworthiness. He will not be self-satisfied or self-complacent. He will often be deeply humbled.

Sanctification, in short, is a practical business. It is not a thing to be talked about, but to be practised. It is not a subject for the closet and the study alone, but for the workshop, the market, the house, and the street.

Some people seem to think that sanctification and the ordinary business of life are incompatible with each other. They separate religion and life into two different compartments. They have their religious life, and they have their ordinary daily life, and they never bring the two together. This is a great mistake.

Godliness is profitable for all things. The Christian is to be holy everywhere, in his shop as in his church, in his family as in his private devotions, in his conduct toward men as in his conduct toward God.

I exhort every reader to remember this. Do not be content with a religion which only shows itself on Sundays and in church. Carry your religion into every part of your life. Be holy at home, holy in business, holy in society, holy in all your ways. This is what God requires, and this is the only religion which will stand the test of the great day.

chapters.title: Chapter IV — The Fight
chapters.content:
"Fight the good fight of faith." — 1 Timothy 6:12

True Christianity is a warfare. The idea of fighting is one which the Bible constantly dwells upon in connection with true religion. It is a point which deserves far more attention than it generally receives.

A Christian is a soldier. Let us settle this firmly in our minds. Let us never forget that the life of a true Christian is a life of warfare. He has enemies to fight — the world, the flesh, and the devil. He must fight with these enemies every day. He will never be free from them as long as he lives.

Let me describe the nature of this Christian warfare.

The enemy against whom we fight is mighty. The world is against us. The prince of this world, the devil, is against us. Our own corrupt nature is against us. These are formidable enemies. They are not to be despised. They are not to be treated lightly.

The fighting we engage in is not with flesh and blood, but with principalities, with powers, with the rulers of the darkness of this world, with spiritual wickedness in high places. (Ephesians 6:12.) The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds. (2 Corinthians 10:4.)

The Christian, then, must be a fighting man. He must always be ready to fight. He must fight every day. He must fight for his faith, his peace, his comfort, his growth in grace, his evidences of conversion.

But let me show you what this fighting involves.

The Christian must fight against sin. He must resist every temptation. He must wrestle against the tendency to pride, to unbelief, to worldliness, to sloth, to covetousness, to sensuality, to self-will. He must be ever on the watch against the wiles of the devil.

The Christian must fight in the strength of the Lord. He does not fight in his own strength. He fights in the strength of the Lord of hosts, and in the power of his might. He draws his weapons from God's armoury — from the Word of God, from prayer, from the sacraments, from public worship.

The Christian must fight with a brave heart. He must not be a coward. He must not give way to fear. He must not run away from the enemy. He must stand firm, and having done all, stand.

The Christian must never lay down his arms. He must fight to the last. He must not say, 'I have fought enough,' or 'I am too old to fight,' or 'I have had victories enough,' or 'I need not watch so carefully now.' He must fight on, day after day, until the time comes when God calls him home.

And the Christian must fight hopefully. He must not be discouraged by failures and defeats. He must remember that Christ has conquered, and that Christ will give him the final victory. He must remember that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, but that God gives the victory in the end to those who trust in him.

I commend this subject to the careful thought of every reader. Are you fighting? Have you taken up the weapons of a Christian soldier? Are you resisting the world, the flesh, and the devil?

I fear that many professing Christians know nothing of this warfare. They have never put on the whole armour of God. They have never learned to wrestle and strive against sin. They are at peace with the world, and at peace with the devil, because they have never declared war against them.

Arise, Christian soldier! Take up the weapons of your warfare! Fight the good fight of faith! Fight, and God will bless you. Fight, and God will give you the victory.

chapters.title: Chapter V — The Cost
chapters.content:
"Count the cost." — Luke 14:28

I want to speak in this chapter about the cost of being a thorough Christian. I am convinced that one great cause of the failings and inconsistencies of many professors of religion is their want of counting the cost of discipleship.

I believe that thousands of persons are received into what are called the visible limits of the church every year who have never been told that there is a cost to be paid, a race to be run, a war to be carried on, a sacrifice to be made in becoming a decided Christian.

I am afraid that the great doctrine of grace and free salvation, when not balanced by other parts of Christian truth, is sometimes so handled as to produce a pernicious effect upon the minds of hearers. Men are told so frequently of the freeness of salvation, and that sinners are not saved by their works, that they sometimes get an impression that it is a very easy thing to be a Christian, and that being saved costs nothing at all.

Now, it is not easy to be a Christian. It costs something to be a decided, thorough, genuine, uncompromising servant of God. This is what I want to press on every reader.

What is the cost of being a real Christian? I will try to answer this question.

It costs self-denial. The first great cost of becoming a true Christian is the giving up of the things which the flesh and the world regard as pleasant. A man who is in earnest about his soul will often have to go against the current of public opinion. He will have to refuse many invitations to join the amusements and dissipations of the world. He will have to bear many a sneer and many a jest from those who do not understand him. He must be content to be unlike the world.

It costs breaking the chains of the world's opinion. This is a great cost. The fear of man is one of the strongest chains by which the devil holds men back from God. To be willing to be singular — to be willing to stand alone — to be willing to be thought peculiar — this is something which many find very hard.

It costs quarrelling with those who are near and dear. This is another great cost. Christ himself warned his disciples that he had come to set a man at variance with his father and his mother and his children and his relatives. There is a time in many a young Christian's life when he finds that his earnestness about religion is a source of grief and trouble to those he loves best on earth.

It costs a constant battle with sin. This also is a great cost. The indulgences of the flesh, the pleasures of sense, the pride of the eye and the pride of life — all these must be given up by the man who will be a true Christian.

But let me say a word on the other side. Are there any compensations for all this cost?

Yes! There are infinite compensations. The peace which Christianity gives the soul, the sense of sins forgiven, the confidence of a filial relation with God, the hope of glory — all these are compensations which outweigh the cost a thousandfold.

The blessedness of knowing that our sins are pardoned, that God is reconciled, that heaven is before us — this is worth more than all the world can give.

Count the cost, I urge every reader. But count the gains also. And when you have counted both, go forward. Take up your cross. Follow Christ. You will never regret it.

chapters.title: Chapter VI — Growth
chapters.content:
"Grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ." — 2 Peter 3:18

I wish to speak in this chapter about growth in grace. It is a subject of great practical importance, and one which is not sufficiently considered.

Growth in grace is the mark of every genuine Christian. Every true believer should grow in grace year by year. He should be a better man, a stronger man, a wiser man, a more useful man, at the end of each year than he was at the beginning. He should know more of God, more of himself, more of his Bible, more of his duty, more of his privileges, than he did before.

I will try to show what growth in grace consists of.

A man grows in grace when he grows in holiness. He hates sin more, and loves righteousness more than he did. He gains more complete victories over temptation. He feels less and less the power of the world upon his heart. He becomes less conformed to the world and more conformed to God.

A man grows in grace when he grows in faith. He trusts God more implicitly. He leans more entirely on Christ. He has less dependence on himself, and more dependence on the Lord. His prayers become more bold and more confident.

A man grows in grace when he grows in love. He loves God more. He loves Christ more. He loves his fellow-Christians more. He loves the souls of men more, and is more earnest in trying to do them good.

A man grows in grace when he grows in humility. He thinks less of himself. He is more sensible of his own unworthiness, his own weakness, his own imperfection. He feels that he is nothing, and that God is all.

A man grows in grace when he grows in thankfulness. He praises God more. He is more deeply sensible of his mercies, and more ready to give God the glory for them.

A man grows in grace when he grows in the spirit of prayer. He prays more, prays better, prays with more faith, prays with more earnestness.

A man grows in grace when he grows in contentment. He is less disturbed by the changes and chances of this mortal life. He has learned to be content in whatever state he is. He has learned that all things work together for good to them that love God.

How can a man grow in grace? He must use the means which God has appointed.

He must use his Bible diligently. He must read it every day. He must search it carefully. He must store it in his memory. The Word of God is the food of the soul.

He must be diligent in prayer. He must pray every day, morning and evening. He must pray both in private and in his family. He must ask God to teach him, and strengthen him, and keep him.

He must be diligent in attending public worship. He must not forsake the assembling of himself together with God's people.

He must watch over his own heart. He must examine himself daily. He must be ever on the watch against pride, and sloth, and worldliness, and unbelief.

And he must have constant recourse to Christ. He must draw all his strength from Christ. He must be ever coming to Christ as the fountain of all grace.

Grow in grace, I urge every reader. Look back on last year and ask yourself whether you have grown. Press forward. Do not be content to stand still. Forget the things that are behind, and reach forward to the things that are before.

chapters.title: Chapter VII — Assurance
chapters.content:
"These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life." — 1 John 5:13

I desire in this chapter to consider the subject of assurance — the full assurance of a believer that he is a child of God.

Is it possible for a man to know that he is a child of God? Is it possible for a man to feel sure that he is saved?

I answer unhesitatingly — Yes. I believe it is not only possible for a man to know that he is in a state of grace, but that God desires every believer to know it.

The text at the head of this chapter speaks for itself. The Apostle John says that he wrote his first Epistle with the express purpose of enabling believers to know that they have eternal life. This implies that such knowledge is attainable.

I affirm boldly that the Scripture contains abundant promises of a knowledge of our own salvation. The whole Epistle of 1 John is written with a view to this end. From beginning to end the Apostle lays down marks by which the true Christian may test his own state.

What are the grounds on which a believer may obtain assurance?

The first ground of assurance is faith in the promises of God. God has made many great and precious promises to those who believe. He has promised that whosoever believes on Christ shall not perish but have eternal life. He has promised that he will never leave nor forsake those who put their trust in him. He has promised that all things shall work together for good to them that love God. The believer who rests on these promises, and believes God at his word, may obtain assurance.

The second ground of assurance is the witness of the Holy Spirit to our own spirits. Paul says that the Spirit itself bears witness with our spirit that we are the children of God. (Romans 8:16.) The Holy Spirit works in the believer's heart a sense of God's fatherly love, and a childlike feeling towards God. This is a witness to the believer's sonship.

The third ground of assurance is the evidence of a changed life. A man who examines his own heart and life, and finds there a love of God, a love of Christ, a love of holiness, a hatred of sin, a longing for heaven — such a man has evidence within himself that he is born of God.

I earnestly desire that every reader who is a true Christian should seek after full assurance. I believe that the want of it is a great hindrance to Christian usefulness and happiness. A man who is not sure that he is saved will be a feeble and half-hearted Christian. A man who is sure that he is saved will be bold, decided, and vigorous.

But let me say plainly that assurance is not the same thing as faith. A man may be a true Christian without having assurance. The thing that is necessary to salvation is faith. Assurance is the fruit of a settled faith.

And let me say that assurance must not be mistaken for presumption. The man who says 'I am sure I shall be saved, whatever I do' is not speaking of the assurance of the Scripture. True assurance is always connected with a holy life and a deepening sense of unworthiness.

Seek assurance, dear reader. Seek it by close walking with God. Seek it by diligent use of Scripture, prayer, and sacrament. Seek it by living near to the cross. And when you have obtained it, hold it fast. It is a precious treasure.
